the Lake Tanganyika record preserves evidence of: (1) a lake level drop prior to 90 ka, (2) a high lake stand between 78 and 72 ka, (3) a lake level decrease at ∼ 65 ka, (4) an increase in biogenic silicate at ∼ 36.8 ka, (5) a decrease in lake level at ∼ 30 ka, (6) a lake level increase at �

(1) Lake Tanganyika was much lower than today prior to ∼90 ka, suggesting a period with very low rainfall; (2) the lake level rose to near modern levels sometime after 78 ka, suggesting an intensification of rainfall, possibly due to an increase in orbital eccentricity; and (3) the lake level dropped again at ∼ 60 ka, possibly due to the intensification of the ITCZ over the Indian Ocean.
Lake Tanganyika experienced a period of aridity prior to 90 ka and that it was a shallow lake sometime between ∼ 90 and ∼ 80 ka.

a better understanding of the mechanisms behind tropical climate in continental regions and how it relates to global climate change.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the climate of Lake Tanganyikan basin is controlled by both regional and global forcing, and that these forcing mechanisms vary in importance over different time intervals.
Lake Tanganyika has responded to global climate change in the past 90 kyr, but that the mechanisms driving these climate changes are not well understood.
the Lake Tanganyika record is consistent with the idea of a global climate reorganization at ∼ 80 ka, but the exact mechanism of this reorganization is not yet understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the climate of East Africa has responded to global climate forcing mechanisms over the past 100,000 years, with a strong influence of the Asian monsoon, but that the mechanisms driving the East African climate system remain poorly understood.

Lake Tanganyika has been responding to climate forcing over the past 100 kyr, including the LGM, and that the timing of these events is consistent with a global climate reorganization, possibly forced by orbital eccentricity.

the Lake Tanganyika record is consistent with the idea that the East African climate is forced primarily by global climate mechanisms, and that the East African monsoon is a response to these mechanisms, and not the cause of them.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Lake Tanganyika record provides a new and valuable window into tropical East African climate change, and that this lake has responded to global climate forcing in a coherent way over the past 60+ kyr.

East African climate change is not a simple function of orbital forcing, but is also affected by global climate dynamics, and that the East African climate system is coherent across the basin, and possibly with other tropical regions.
Lake Tanganyika has a long history of responding to climate changes in the region and that the timing of these events is consistent with global climate forcing.
